name: Serpentine Arête

pitch_detail.notes: Up an obvious dihedral past two trees with webbing to a large terrace; some parties end up on harder 5th class here by mistake
Crack systems and a small dihedral toward the crux; a lichen-covered slab section feels sketchy
The two consecutive crux pitches: a finger crack into a splitter hand crack, then a dihedral with bomber finger locks; link with a 70m rope
Ridge-crest scrambling, a short downclimb, sandy gully to the summit — mostly simul-climbable

rappels: Typically none — walk off via a traverse to Backbone Ridge, then descend Snow Creek Glacier (boot-skiing) and Aasgard Pass
descent_text: From the summit, most parties head down the loose sandy gully shared with the top of Backbone Ridge, boot-ski or downclimb the upper Snow Creek Glacier snowfield where present, then traverse to Aasgard Pass (7,841 ft) and descend its steep, loose talus/scree back to Colchuck Lake. Crampons and an ice axe are important for this descent whenever snow/ice remain on the upper mountain or in Aasgard Pass. Some parties instead reverse via Colchuck Glacier/Col — route-find carefully, as the descent gully is loose and cliffs out if the wrong line is taken.
approach: From the Stuart Lake Trailhead (FR 7601), hike the Colchuck Lake Trail ~4 mi / 2,280 ft gain to Colchuck Lake (5,574 ft). Round the lake's west shore to its south end, boulder-hop onto the Colchuck Glacier's lateral moraine, and traverse it toward the orange-colored rock marking the route start; 4th-class ledges lead up to a snow finger and the base of the technical climbing. Roughly 3 hours car-to-base at a brisk pace.
overview: A long, high-quality granite line up the right (west) side of Dragontail's north face, roughly 200 ft right of Backbone Ridge, following corners and crack systems to two sustained 5.8 crux pitches before ridge scrambling to the summit.
beta: Climbs an obvious dihedral system past two trees with webbing to a large terrace, then crack systems and a small dihedral to the crux — two consecutive 5.8 pitches (a finger crack into a splitter hand crack, then a dihedral with bomber finger locks) that can be linked with a 70m rope. Above the crux the route stays on the ridge crest with mostly 3rd-4th class/low-5th scrambling, a short downclimb, and a sandy gully to the summit area. All of the technical climbing is on solid rock even though the low-5th-class sections are loose.
face: North face, right (NW) side — above the Colchuck Glacier
